hints: Focus on the two separate tests here, a compound must be chiral and also acidic enough to release CO2 from carbonate.
Remember only a carboxylic acid group, $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, is acidic enough to react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, so rule out any alcohol or ester straight away.
Now look for a carbon with four different groups attached in the remaining acid structures to find the true chiral centre.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two conditions**

Think like a detective with two clues. First, chiral means a carbon with four different groups and no plane of symmetry. Second, reaction with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give $\text{CO}_2$ means a carboxylic acid must be present.

$$\text{2RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{2RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$

**Filter by acidity**

Alcohols like in B are too weakly acidic and esters like in C have no $\text{-OH}$ to donate, so they cannot liberate $\text{CO}_2$. That leaves only the molecules containing $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups.

Acid needed: $\text{R-CO}_2\text{H}$

**Test the acids for chirality**

Compound A is a planar alkene, $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CH=CH-CO}_2\text{H}$, with no carbon bearing four different single groups, so it is achiral. Compound D is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(Br)CO}_2\text{H}$, where C-2 is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, four different groups, so it is chiral and is the answer.

options.A: This is cis-butenedioic acid (maleic acid). It has two $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups so it does react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give $\text{CO}_2$, but it is achiral because the $\text{C=C}$ is planar and there is no carbon with four different groups.
options.B: This is 1-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol, a tertiary alcohol. Alcohols are much weaker acids than carbonic acid so they do not react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$. It fails the acidity test even though the C-1 centre has four different attachments.
options.C: This is an ester, $\text{HCO}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)(CH}_2\text{Br)}$. The central carbon is chiral (bonded to H, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ and $\text{OCHO}$), but esters have no acidic proton and do not react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give $\text{CO}_2$.
options.D: This is 2-bromobutanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(Br)CO}_2\text{H}$. It contains $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ so it reacts with carbonate to release $\text{CO}_2$, and C-2 is bonded to four different groups ($\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) so it is chiral.
